clue.text: Chap regularly knocked back beer in plant

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so only every other letter is kept
a drink knocked back is downed, and here the word is turned back to front

blocks.note: the first and third letters of the word
a pint is a measure of beer in a British pub

explanation.surface: A man downs a beer while sitting among the greenery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' reads as drinking the beer, which suits the pub picture, but it means the beer's word runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Catnip is a herb of the mint family whose scent excites cats, so it is a specific example of a plant.

clue.text: A grassy area cut for match

indicators.note: a thing that is cut has been shortened, so its final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: taken as written
a stretch of public lawn, such as the common in the middle of a village, has this name

explanation.surface: A patch of turf is mown ready for a sports fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' looks like a cricket or football game to suit the grass, but it is the verb: to correspond.
explanation.definitionFit: Two accounts that match are consistent with each other, which is the verb sense of being in accord or corresponding.

clue.text: Large island freshly minted old coin?

blocks.note: something freshly minted is brand new
the guinea was an old British gold coin worth 21 shillings

explanation.surface: A big island described as a newly struck antique coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freshly minted' fits the coin of the surface; it simply means new. The guinea was a British coin last struck in 1814.
explanation.definitionFit: New Guinea in the Pacific is the second-largest island in the world, shared between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea.

clue.text: Constant speed for raider

blocks.note: pi is the mathematical constant relating a circle's circumference to its diameter
a rate is a speed, as in a rate of knots

explanation.surface: A raider needs to keep up a steady pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constant' looks like an adjective describing the speed, but it is the noun: a fixed value in mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirate is a seafarer who attacks and robs ships, so the word is a synonym for a raider at sea.

clue.text: Fair energy attributed to dormice when excited

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sleepy dormice show a reasonable amount of energy once they are roused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' could be a funfair or pale skin, but it is the middling sense, as in a fair attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair can mean only moderately good, neither poor nor excellent, which is exactly what mediocre describes.

clue.text: Pedestrian — where one shouldn’t be?

definitions.note: a phrase naming a place rather than an adjective

blocks.note: first meaning: dull, unadventurous, ordinary
second meaning: read literally, the spot on a street a walker should avoid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' first reads as a person on foot, which sets up the second half; then it turns out to be the adjective meaning dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Music or politics called middle-of-the-road is moderate and bland, the same sense as pedestrian meaning uninspired.

clue.text: Shift time for equestrian event

blocks.note: a shift is a simple straight dress
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to move the schedule of a horse show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shift time' reads as rescheduling, but 'Shift' is the noun for a loose dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is a competitive discipline in which a horse performs precise trained movements, one of the events in equestrian sport.

clue.text: Eye, tongue, but not head

indicators.note: the head is the front, so excluding it drops the opening letter

blocks.note: Coptic is a language, the liturgical tongue of Egypt's Coptic Church

explanation.surface: A list of body parts, eye and tongue, with the head left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites anatomy, but 'tongue' means a language here; Coptic loses its C.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic is an informal or humorous noun for the eye, from its adjective sense relating to vision.

clue.text: Wicked crimes in evidence initially, look to more innocent times?

indicators.note: wicked suggests something twisted or perverted from its proper form, so the letters are reworked
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Faced with proof of terrible offences, someone longs for a more innocent past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' sits naturally with crimes as an adjective, but it is the anagram signal. The definition is playful: looking back to times before the crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to recall the past fondly, and the question mark admits that earlier days need not truly be more innocent.

clue.text: Tie cross in part of castle

blocks.note: a tie in a game is a draw
to bridge something is to span or cross it

explanation.surface: Someone knots a crucifix or ribbon somewhere inside a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tie' and 'cross' suggest fastening and a crucifix, but they are a drawn result and the verb to span.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawbridge is the hinged bridge over a castle moat, raised for defence, so it is a feature belonging to a castle.

clue.text: Domestic thanks yours truly

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thank you
yours truly is a jokey way of saying oneself

explanation.surface: The sign-off of a homely thank-you letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domestic' looks like household matters, but it means an animal that is not wild.
explanation.definitionFit: A domestic animal is one kept by people and accustomed to them, which is the sense of tame as opposed to wild.

clue.text: Target surrounded by genuine defence

indicators.note: a thing surrounded by another is enclosed within it on all sides

blocks.note: a butt is a target, as in the butt of a joke
genuine means real

explanation.surface: A target is ringed by a true line of defenders.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a military scene; a butt is also the mound behind a shooting target.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebuttal is an argument contradicting an accusation, so it serves as a defence in debate or court.

clue.text: Short amount of time on shoulder of leader?

definitions.note: a positional phrase rather than a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: a sixtieth of a minute
in a race, a runner on the leader's shoulder is just behind in the next place

explanation.surface: Something briefly perched on the boss's shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing, to sit on someone's shoulder is to run just behind them, ready to pass.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a sixtieth of a minute and the position immediately after first in a race or ranking.

clue.text: Turn and trip

blocks.note: first meaning: to rotate rapidly
second meaning: a short drive or ride for pleasure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn and trip' sounds like stumbling; each word is instead a separate meaning, the second a jaunt in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers whirling round on an axis and also a brief outing, as in taking a car for a spin.

clue.text: Animal hiding gold vessel in tree

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a cup is a drinking vessel
a pine is a coniferous tree

explanation.surface: A creature stashes a golden goblet up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a squirrel hoarding treasure; the hiding is done by the tree, which wraps around the gold vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The porcupine is a large rodent covered in protective quills, a specific example of an animal.

clue.text: Rating so shocking for player

indicators.note: something shocking jolts and disturbs, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sportsperson receives an appalling performance score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests sport alongside a rating, but it is a musician.
explanation.definitionFit: An organist plays the organ, so the word is a specific kind of player of a musical instrument.

clue.text: Terrible man climbing over part of wall — safe to go through?

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means going upward, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Ivan the Terrible was the sixteenth-century Russian tsar
a gable is the triangular upper part of an end wall under a pitched roof

explanation.surface: A dreadful man scales a wall, and someone wonders whether the gap is safe to pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible man' looks like any villain but points to Ivan the Terrible. 'Over' places him above the gable in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A navigable river or channel is one wide and deep enough for vessels to pass through it safely.

clue.text: Dish served to convict?

blocks.note: surface reading: a meal handed out in a prison canteen
setter's reading: what a convict serves is a jail term, and the British slang for a jail term is also a breakfast oat dish

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, doing porridge means serving time in prison, so a convict 'serves' it as well as eats it.
explanation.definitionFit: Porridge is a hot breakfast dish of boiled oats, and the slang sense of a prison sentence makes the convict fitting.

clue.text: Escape, off on holiday

blocks.note: a break is a short holiday
off means away or out, as in going off for the day

explanation.surface: Getting away from it all by going on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'off on holiday' puts the first piece after the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To break out is to escape from confinement, as prisoners do, so the phrasal verb is a synonym of escape.

clue.text: Challenge wife, in scene

blocks.note: to vie is to compete or contend
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Someone confronts their wife in the middle of a public row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a scene' colours the surface as a quarrel; 'scene' here is a landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene can be a landscape or vista seen from a place, which is what a view is.

clue.text: Concealed, cryptic over there partially completed

indicators.note: a task partially completed is only partly done, so only a portion of the letters that follow is used

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word, all of the second, and the first of the third

explanation.surface: A cryptic crossword left half-done and hidden away over there.
explanation.walkthrough: The self-referential 'cryptic' invites thinking of the puzzle itself, but it is just carrier letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Covert means secret or not openly shown, the same sense as concealed, as in a covert operation.

clue.text: Three months for accountant?

definitions.note: a person, while the answer is read as one who sums

blocks.note: first meaning: the warm season, roughly June to August in the north
second meaning: read as one who sums, someone who adds up figures

explanation.surface: A quarter-year allotted to the bookkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: Accountants work in quarters, so the surface suggests a financial period; the question mark flags the invented sense, a person who adds things up.
explanation.definitionFit: The season spans about a quarter of the year, and the coined noun from the verb to sum names someone who totals figures.

clue.text: US state cardinal discussed?

indicators.note: something discussed is talked about, so it is the spoken sound that counts

blocks.note: cardinal means chief or principal, as in a cardinal rule

explanation.surface: Churchmen debating which American state a cardinal comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' tempts as a churchman or a red bird; it is the adjective meaning most important.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine is the north-eastern New England state of the United States, bordering Canada.

clue.text: Left stuck in one revolving door, let out

indicators.note: something revolving turns round like a wheel, so the last letter comes round to the front
a thing stuck in another is lodged inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for left
a gate is a door in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: Someone trapped in a revolving door is finally released.
explanation.walkthrough: Rotating ONE by one letter gives EON, and L goes inside it. 'Let out' looks like freeing the trapped person, but it is the tailor's sense of lengthening a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: To let out clothing is to lengthen or widen it, so the phrase is a synonym of making something longer.

clue.text: A little beaut, a serious stunner!

indicators.note: a little of something is only a small portion of it, so only a stretch of these words is used

blocks.note: the end of the first word, the middle word, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Admiring a small but seriously gorgeous person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stunner' reads as a beautiful person to match 'beaut'; it is a device that stuns. A Taser is an electroshock weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A Taser fires darts carrying an electric charge to incapacitate someone, so it is literally a stunning device.

clue.text: Fruit that will never take off?

definitions.text: Fruit that will never take off?

blocks.clueFragment: Fruit that will never take off?
blocks.note: surface reading: a fruit that will never become popular
setter's reading: the fruit shares its name with a flightless New Zealand bird

explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests commercial success, but it means flying; the fruit is named after a bird that cannot fly.
explanation.definitionFit: The kiwi fruit, or Chinese gooseberry, was marketed under the name of New Zealand's national bird, which is flightless.

clue.text: Make every effort to see bonds broken

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tries hard to watch their chains being smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To see' reads as a purpose link joining definition to wordplay, but its letters are part of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To make every effort is to try as hard as possible, which is the idiom of giving one's utmost.

clue.text: Separate bags in any event for minister

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it in a sack, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: to rend is to tear apart
ever means at any time or in any case

explanation.surface: Sorting luggage for a government minister at a function.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' looks like luggage and 'minister' like a politician; one is the verb to enclose, the other a cleric.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverend is a member of the clergy, and minister is the usual word for a Protestant cleric.

clue.text: Politician punched by that man — possible explanation?

indicators.note: a punch makes a hole that something goes into, so one piece is driven inside another

blocks.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party
he is the pronoun for that man

explanation.surface: A politician gets hit by a man, and someone guesses why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punched by' sounds like assault, but it means the man's word is driven into the politician's.
explanation.definitionFit: A theory is a proposed account of why something happens, not yet proven, which is a possible explanation.
